title: workload-fingerprint-catalog-and-repeatable-seedbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a practical playbook for creating canonical workload fingerprints ("traffic cards"), running repeatable throughput experiments, and maintaining seed hygiene across the serving runtime team. It complements the formal benchmark harness docs by focusing on cataloging real workload shapes and a compact reproducible run recipe for everyday experiments.

High-level goals:
- Define a small, versioned library of traffic cards that cover our common production shapes (chat short-turns, long-completions, instruction-heavy, embedding-heavy bulk loads).
- Provide a deterministic recipe to reproduce a benchmark run end-to-end (input pool, RNG seeds, client pacing, warmup strategy, env pinning).
- Capture a minimal telemetry set and failure-mode checklist to speed triage when runs are noisy.

What is a traffic card (workload fingerprint)?
- A compact spec that fully describes the client-side workload characteristics needed to reproduce a benchmark. Each card contains: arrival distribution (Poisson/constant/bursty), target concurrency or rps, seq-length distribution (prompt + gen tokens), prompt mix (named buckets with relative proportions), stop conditions, client-side batching/config, and optional KV/prefix state behavior.
- Store each card as a small JSON + README in the canonical catalog. Name convention: tc/{familily}-{median-seq}-{arrival}-{year}.{revision} e.g. tc/chat-32-poisson-2024.v1

Traffic card library (examples):
1) tc/chat-16-poisson-2024.v1
   - Arrival: Poisson lambda tuned to 400 requests/min
   - Concurrency target: soft 60 concurrency
   - Prompt mix: 70% short helper prompts (mean 8 tokens), 30% follow-ups (mean 40 tokens)
   - Generation tokens: sample from empirical distribution (1..128), mean 16
   - Client batching: max_batch_tokens=4096, per-request token cap=256
   - Warmup hint: 5k sample priming requests with cached KV none

2) tc/longgen-1024-burst-2024.v1
   - Arrival: deterministic bursts of 8 concurrent requests every 10s
   - Concurrency target: instantaneous spikes to 120
   - Prompt mix: 100% long prompts (median prompt 280 tokens)
   - Generation tokens: tail distribution, mean 1024
   - Warmup hint: 2 full-sequence priming runs (fills KV cache)

3) tc/embed-batch-bulk-2024.v1
   - Arrival: sustained high throughput (rps=1200) with small payloads
   - Concurrency target: auto-scale to keep latency p95 < 50ms
   - Prompt mix: fixed 512-dim embedding inputs sampled from corpus
   - Client batching: group up to 512 embeddings per call

Run recipe: a minimal reproducible benchmark (copy/paste friendly)
- Preconditions: pin model to exact version and quantization profile (e.g., open-llm/abc@v2024-11-08+q4_0), pin runtime image, collect commit SHAs for serving runtime and loadgen.
- Inputs: a hashed prompt pool file: prompts.txt and prompts.sha256. Always store the prompts.sha256 alongside results.
- RNG: choose explicit RNG seed (e.g., --seed 13721). Document in metadata.
- Cache state: decide initial KV state: empty | prefilled-with-priming. If priming, record primer file used and number of priming tokens.
- Client start sequence:
  1) Clear runtime caches (if possible).
  2) Start observability & metrics exporter.
  3) Run priming phase: run N=sample_count (default 500) requests from primer set with same concurrency target used in experiment to populate common caches.
  4) Wait stabilizationDelay (tunable, default 30s) to let metrics settle.
  5) Start measurement window for a fixed duration (recommended 30m for stable numbers, 5m for quick smoke).

Concrete loadgen command (example using internal loadgen v2):
python -m loadgen.run \
  --card tc/chat-16-poisson-2024.v1.json 
  --model open-llm/abc@v2024-11-08+q4_0 
  --seed 13721 
  --priming-file primer-500.txt 
  --priming-requests 500 
  --stabilize 30 
  --measurement-interval 1800 
  --capture-batching-distribution 
  --out results/run-2024-11-15-chat16.json

Essential telemetry to capture every run (minimum set):
- Request-level: start_ts, end_ts, response_bytes, tokens_generated, prompt_length, generated_length, status_code, client_latency_ms, server_latency_ms (if available).
- Aggregate: total_tokens, tokens_per_second, requests_per_second, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, success_rate.
- Host/GPU: GPU_util_pct, GPU_mem_used_mb, CPU_user_pct, net_bytes_in/out, queue_length, inflight_batches, batch_size_histogram.
- Runtime internals (if enabled): kv_cache_hit_rate, average_batch_fill, kernel_choice, kernel_time_ms.

Repro checklist (must be in run metadata):
- prompts.sha256 = <hash>
- loadgen commit = <sha>
- serving-runtime image = <sha/tag>
- model id + weights sha = <id@sha>
- seed = <int>
- card = <tc name + version>
- priming-file + priming-requests = <file, int>
- timezone + clock sync check (ntp)
- node list + instance types used

Warmup strategies (practical notes):
- Micro-warm: small number (50-200) of short requests across nodes to warm up kernels and JIT paths. Good for very quick smoke runs.
- Full prime: send representative requests that exercise large KV cache & sequence lengths (useful when measuring throughput for longgen).
- Continuous ramp: ramp RPS from 1% -> 100% over a short window (60–120s) to allow autoscalers and runtime to settle.
- Repeatable priming: use the same primer file + seed every time. Store in /catalog/primers with a hash and brief description.

Common variance sources and triage steps:
- High variance between runs: check prompt pool entropy (hash distribution), verify RNG seed used, compare batch_size_histogram between runs.
- Sudden p99 spikes with stable median: look for heterogeneous sequence lengths forming large batches, or background GC on host, or device thermal throttling. Correlate with GPU_util and CPU steal.
- Throughput regressions after infra change: confirm kernel selection logs (kernel_choice) and quantization profile pinned. If kernel changed, re-run small compatibility smoke to isolate.
- Intermittent timeouts: check rate limiter traces, backpressure metrics, and queue_length -- may be client-side or internal queue saturation.

Data capture & storage:
- Write raw request-level traces to compressed ndjson with a run metadata header. Example file: results/run-2024-11-15-chat16.ndjson.gz and results/run-2024-11-15-chat16.meta.json
- Keep a single-line summary CSV for quick dashboards: run_id, card, model, seed, duration_s, avg_tps, p95_lat_ms, total_tokens.

Acceptance / stable-run criteria (gating for committing numbers to benchmark dashboard):
- Measurement window >= 15m (prefer 30m)
- Coefficient of variation for avg TPS across sliding 1m windows < 3%
- p95/p99 stable across last 10% of window (no >10% drift)
- No infra events (node restarts, OOMs, throttling) during run

Result reporting template (store with run):
- run_id: <uuid>
- card: <tc name + version>
- model: <id@sha>
- seed: <int>
- primed: true|false
- duration_s: <int>
- avg_tps: <float>
- p50/p90/p95/p99: <ms>
- total_tokens: <int>
- notes: free-text

Failure-mode playbook (quick actions):
- If large variance: re-run with identical seed and prime. If variance remains, increase measurement duration and collect kernel traces.
- If throughput unexpectedly low: verify network path and instance sizing, check that autoscaler is healthy and that GPU mem pressure isn't causing OOMs and serial fallbacks.
- If batch sizes collapse to 1 frequently: check arrival jitter and client pacing; enable client-side batching guards (min_batch_fill_time).

Housekeeping and ownership:
- Catalog owner: eng-serving-runtime (primary: Aisha Patel). Review cadence: quarterly or on major runtime/model changes.
- Primer files: store under /catalog/primers with descriptive names and checksums.
- Retention: keep full run artifacts for 90 days, summaries in dashboard indefinitely.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Add a small CI job that validates each traffic card with a 5m smoke run on a cheap test cluster and records the baseline.
- Convert top-3 cards to canonical YAML and add to confluence page referenced above.
- Investigate automating kernel_choice capture during priming so we can detect silent changes across runtime images.

Notes to self / open questions:
- How to succinctly represent mixed workloads with cross-correlation (e.g., embeddings + chat bursts)? Consider a composite-card format but keep the API minimal.
- Should priming be mandated for all longgen cards? Operational cost vs. reproducibility tradeoff needs doc.

Attachments (examples):
- primer-500.txt (sha256: e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb924)
- tc/chat-16-poisson-2024.v1.json (inline spec)
- sample results CSV row: run-2024-11-15-chat16,chat-16-poisson-2024.v1,open-llm/abc@v2024-11-08+q4_0,13721,1800,42.3,76,120,180,320000

If you run a noisy experiment, paste the run_id in #bench-results and include the results meta file link. We'll iterate on the card or warmup recipe until the acceptance criteria are met.

End of doc.
